newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Six dead as Montserrat volcano claims first victims.
newsitem.headline: Six dead as Montserrat volcano claims first victims.

text.p: Rescue workers on Thursday found the bodies of six people killed in a deadly blast of hot gases and rocks from a volcano on the Caribbean island of Montserrat.
"There were six people (dead)," said a spokeswoman at the island's Emergency Operations Center.

The dead, who were not immediately identified, were the first victims of Soufriere Hills volcano since it roared to life in a rain of ash, rock and smoke on July 18, 1995, ending nearly four centuries of virtual dormancy.

Several other people remained unaccounted for on Thursday as rescue workers, including Dutch sailors, mounted a house-to-house search of seven villages, all of them in the evacuated "danger zone," that were affected by Wednesday's blast.

"There has been considerable destruction of buildings including houses in the area of the flows," the government said in a statement. The flows almost reached the island's only airport, which was closed.

Government officials said at least 13 people had been airlifted to safety by search teams on Thursday, in addition to 19 rescued on Wednesday. Several of those were taken to the island's hospital suffering from burns.

Between 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. EDT (1700 and 1800 GMT) on Wednesday, part of the giant dome of volcanic material that has been growing inside the volcano collapsed, dousing much of the island with ash and sending a pyroclastic flow -- a fast-moving rain of superheated gases, ash and rock -- toward the eastern side of the island.

Authorities said seven villages along the flow burst into flames, all of them in the danger zone, which has been evacuated for 14 months. A few of the people affected were residents who had refused to evacuate. Others were farmers returning to feed animals and check on their property.

"It is an almost impossible task to police that area," Montserrat's Chief Minister Bertrand Osborne told reporters. "Check points were erected, people were told not to go past the checkpoints and we were criticized for that, but people always found ways of getting inside."

Scientists monitoring the volcano warned of another increase in volcanic activity on Thursday afternoon, with the possibility of more serious pyroclastic flows. They said residents should be alert and avoid the danger zone.
"We have actually been warned that the volcano could produce further large pyroclastic flows," Claude Hogan, a Montserrat government spokesman, said.
Montserrat's airport, which was evacuated on Wednesday, remained closed and was not expected to be opened for a least a couple of days, Hogan said.
Crewmen from a Royal Dutch Navy ship docked in Montserrat were assisting with the search. A British Royal Navy ship stationed in the Caribbean was heading to the island.
Montserrat's population has shrunk from 11,000 to 6,800 people since the volcanic eruptions began in 1995.
